title: Change Control
sequence: Assess and Implement Changes runs from the start of the project to its completion; changes can occur at any stage. Approved changes are implemented in Executing.

header.html: Business Environment domain (26%) · Task 3 Manage and control changes — execute the change control process · communicate the status of proposed changes · implement approved changes to the project · update project documentation to reflect changes

Topic 24 (implementing approved changes in execution) · Topic 15 (scope control, creep, gold plating) · Topic 16 and 17 (schedule and cost baselines) · Topic 12 (governance, CCB authority) · Topic 22 (contract changes) · Topic 28 (variance triggers) · Topic 30 (issues) · Topic 32 (organizational change management, a different subject) · Topic 33 (external changes)

Governance domain §2.1.6.8 Assess and Implement Changes (predictive §2.1.6.8.1 and adaptive §2.1.6.8.2; Figure 2-11) · Section 4 artifacts (change management plan, configuration management plan, change requests, approved change requests, change log, baselines and baseline updates) · Section 5 tools (change control tools, integrated change control, backlog management, data analysis, decision-making)
Assess and Implement Changes runs from the start of the project to its completion; changes can occur at any stage. Approved changes are implemented in Executing.

in PMBOK 8 the change management plan sets up the change control board (CCB), its authority and the change control system. Change management in the glossary means the structured approach for moving people and organizations from a current to a future state (organizational change, Topic 32). Do not confuse the two.
[Beyond PMBOK 8] = exam-relevant, but PMBOK 8 does not spell it out (ECO wording, common exam practice, mock-exam style).

html:
1Core Concepts and Definitions

Term Meaning
Change request A formal proposal to modify a document, deliverable or baseline; any stakeholder may request one; may be internal or external
Types Corrective action (bring performance back in line), preventive action (avoid a future problem), defect repair (fix a nonconformance), updates (modify or add to approved content)
Change control Process by which modifications to documents, deliverables or baselines are identified, documented, approved or rejected
Integrated change control Managing changes in a coordinated way: evaluate requests, analyze impact across the project, decide, document and communicate
Change control board (CCB) A formally chartered group (also steering committee or project board) that reviews, evaluates, approves, defers or rejects changes and records and communicates decisions
Change management plan Establishes the CCB, documents the extent of its authority and describes how the change control system works
Configuration management plan Procedures for tracking project artifacts and monitoring and controlling changes to them: which artifacts are configuration items, how changes are recorded and reported, so the product stays consistent
Configuration control vs change control Configuration control specifies deliverables and processes; change control identifies, documents and approves or rejects changes to documents, deliverables or baselines
Change log Comprehensive list of submitted changes with status and disposition
Approved change request A request processed under the change management plan and approved, deferred or rejected; approved ones are implemented through Manage Project Execution
Baseline The approved version of a work product changeable only through formal change control (scope, schedule, cost; together the performance measurement baseline)
Variation order / contract change A formal change to contract scope, price or time (Topic 22)
Emergency change Beyond PMBOK 8 A change needed immediately (safety, security, outage); handled by a fast path with delegated authority and documented afterward

2The Assess and Implement Changes Process

Purpose: manage changes to scope, product scope, plan components and documents so the project stays aligned with its objectives and constraints. The degree of change request management depends on the scope and complexity of the project, contract requirements and the development approach.

Aspect Detail
Inputs Change management plan, configuration management plan, scope, schedule and cost baselines; basis of estimates, change log, requirements traceability matrix, risk report; work performance reports; change requests; EEFs, OPAs
Tools Expert judgment; change control tools; data analysis (alternative analysis, cost-benefit analysis); decision-making (voting, autocratic, multicriteria decision analysis); meetings; integrated change control; backlog management
Outputs Approved change requests, plan updates (any component), document updates (change log and others)

2.1 Predictive approaches

  • Not formally controlled until baselines exist. Once there is a baseline, all changes go through the formal process.
  • The configuration management plan says which artifacts are under configuration control; changes to them need a formal change request.
  • Changes may start verbally but must be documented in writing and entered in the change or configuration management system.
  • Requests typically include estimated schedule and cost impacts before approval.
  • If a request affects a baseline, integrated change control applies.
  • Each request is approved, deferred or rejected by a designated person (for example the sponsor or the project manager) as defined in the plan or organizational procedures; the figure also shows "more information".
  • A CCB or project board may be involved. While awaiting the decision, keep executing planned work and keep analyzing the impact and risks of accepting or rejecting.
  • Approved changes may need new or updated cost estimates, schedule adjustments, resource requirements and risk assessments, and updates to the plan and documents. Customer or sponsor approval may be needed after CCB approval unless they sit on the CCB.
  • Monitor the results to confirm the change delivered the intended effect.

2.2 Adaptive approaches

  • Change is managed mainly through backlog management, not formal change requests: changes are continuously assessed and prioritized through the iterative cycle.
  • A proposed change is recorded as a product backlog item; an impact analysis evaluates its effect and sets its priority.
  • There is typically no formal approval: any proposed change can be added. A lower priority means the change is effectively deferred; not adding it (or removing it) means it is rejected.
  • The product owner orders the backlog by value, dependencies and constraints (Topic 15).

3Execute the Change Control Process (ECO)

Steps:

  1. Receive and log the request in writing; give it an ID, requester, date and status in the change log.
  2. Assess impact across all domains (diagram below); estimate effects on schedule and cost; check the business case and compliance.
  3. Develop options and recommend: implement, modify, defer or reject; use cost-benefit and multicriteria analysis.
  4. Decide at the right level: the project manager within tolerance and authority; the CCB, sponsor or customer beyond it; record the rationale.
  5. Communicate the decision (section 4).
  6. Implement approved changes through Manage Project Execution (section 5).
  7. Verify that the change achieved its purpose and close it in the log.

Governing principles:

  • Never implement an unapproved change. Even a free improvement, a harmless deviation (a higher-capacity part) or a verified fix is a change: assess its impact and submit it through change control; passing tests does not replace configuration review. If it was already made, submit it retroactively and decide.
  • Corrections of baseline errors (a wrong unit, a missed dependency) are changes to the baseline and go through change control.
  • Scope creep and gold plating are uncontrolled changes (Topic 15).
  • Authority matters: know who may approve what (thresholds in the change management plan or governance framework, Topic 12). If none is defined for a decision above your authority, define it with the sponsor.
  • Changes that affect the business case or external commitments need the sponsor or governance (revalidate value).
  • Do not freeze progress: continue planned work while a decision is pending.

4Communicate the Status of Proposed Changes (ECO)

  • Keep the change log current with status for every request: submitted, under assessment, approved, deferred, rejected, implemented.
  • Tell the requester the decision and rationale, including deferred and rejected requests (PMBOK 8 requires deferred or rejected requests to be communicated to the requester).
  • Inform affected stakeholders and the team of what changed and what it means for them (scope, dates, cost, roles); update the communications plan if needed.
  • Report pending and approved changes in status reports and dashboards (change count, cumulative effect on baselines) (Topic 28).
  • Give CCB members clear packages: description, impact analysis, options, recommendation, risks.
  • In adaptive work, show the backlog and its ordering openly so people see where their request stands; explain trade-offs when something is deferred.

5Implement Approved Changes (ECO)

Approved changes are implemented through Manage Project Execution (Topic 24): corrective actions, preventive actions, defect repairs and updates.

  1. Update the plan components and baselines (scope, schedule, cost; the performance measurement baseline) and funding requirements if needed; re-baseline only through the approved change.
  2. Adjust resources, procurement and contracts (amendments or variation orders, new estimates).
  3. Update the risk register (new or changed risks, reserve use).
  4. Brief the team and stakeholders; train if the change affects how work is done.
  5. Implement and test; verify results; confirm acceptance criteria still hold.
  6. Monitor the effect (did the change deliver the benefit?) and record lessons.

6Update Project Documentation to Reflect Changes (ECO)

An approval is not finished until the documents reflect it. For example, if a design change is approved and the build team starts the work, the drawings, specifications and schedule must be updated.

Update Examples
Baselines and plans Scope baseline (statement, WBS, dictionary), schedule baseline, cost baseline, related management plans
Requirements and design Requirements documentation and traceability matrix, specifications, drawings, backlog and acceptance criteria
Registers and logs Change log, risk register, assumption log, issue log, stakeholder register, lessons learned register
Schedule and cost records Project schedule, forecasts, funding requirements
Contracts Amendments and procurement documentation
Configuration records Versions, status of configuration items, verification
  • Version control and a controlled repository: one authoritative version; everyone works from the current one.
  • Consistency across documents: the same change reflected everywhere (schedule, budget, scope, risks).
  • Communicate the new versions to those affected.

7Configuration Management and Change Control Tools

  • Configuration management (supported by change control tools): identify configuration items, record and report their status, and perform configuration item verification and audits, so that the product configuration is defined and verified, changes are managed and accountability is kept.
  • Change management activities supported by tools: identify and select change items, document them as change requests, decide (review, approve, reject, defer), track registration, assessment, approval and communication, and manage requests and decisions for the CCB.
  • Choose tools by stakeholder needs and organizational constraints (manual or automated).

8Change in Adaptive and Hybrid Work

  • Backlog changes are normal: the product owner reorders by value; frequent customer feedback and market learning mean the roadmap and backlog are updated regularly (do not freeze a year-old roadmap).
  • Protect the iteration: new requests from executives go to the backlog through the product owner; the project manager represents the team's capacity.
  • Formal approval above contract or governance thresholds: for example, a contract requires approval for scope changes above 10% of effort; routine backlog changes flow normally and those above the threshold go through formal approval.
  • Hybrid: formal control for the baselined envelope (milestones, committed scope, budget, regulatory or contractual commitments); the backlog adapts inside it.
  • Impact analysis still happens in adaptive work; it is lighter, not absent.

9Predictive vs Agile vs Hybrid

Predictive Agile / adaptive Hybrid
Mechanism Change request, impact analysis, CCB or designated approver, baseline update Backlog item, impact analysis, product owner prioritization Formal control for the baselined envelope; backlog inside
Approval Formal: approved, deferred, rejected No formal approval; priority decides (lower = deferred, not added = rejected) Both; thresholds trigger formal approval
Record Change log, configuration records Backlog and its history; decision notes Both
Baselines Scope, schedule and cost baselines change only through approved requests Baseline set per iteration; changes between iterations Baselines for commitments only
Speed Slower, more controlled Continuous Mixed

10Tailoring, Interactions and Checking Results

  • Tailor the formality, thresholds and board membership to project size, complexity, contract terms, regulation and approach; a small project may delegate most decisions to the PM or sponsor; a regulated one needs a formal CCB.
  • Interactions: changes touch scope, schedule, finance, quality, resources, risk and stakeholders; they interact with governance (authority), procurement (contract changes), compliance, and benefits (business case).
  • Check results (Table 2-6): predictive projects have a change log showing changes with impact on scope, schedule, finance, stakeholders, resources and risk; adaptive projects use a backlog showing the rate of accomplishing scope, the rate of adding new scope, and the prioritization and inclusion of stakeholder feedback.

11Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

  1. No unapproved changes: even free, beneficial or tested ones go through change control; if made already, submit them now.
  2. Assess impact first (all domains, schedule and cost estimates), then decide; do not approve or reject blindly.
  3. Document in writing even if the request arrives verbally; log everything.
  4. Know the authority level: within tolerance the PM decides; beyond it the CCB, sponsor or customer. Define missing thresholds with the sponsor.
  5. Keep working while waiting for the decision; analyze impact and risk meanwhile.
  6. Communicate all outcomes, including deferred and rejected requests.
  7. Implement and update everything: schedule, drawings, backlog and documents must reflect the approved change.
  8. Baseline corrections are changes and need change control.
  9. Agile change goes through the backlog and the product owner; lower priority means deferred, not added means rejected; formal approval only above contract or governance thresholds.
  10. A change that threatens the business case goes to the sponsor or governance; revalidate value.
  11. Do not confuse the PMBOK 8 change management plan (CCB and change control) with organizational change management.
  12. Change vs issue vs risk: a change request modifies a baseline or document; an issue is a current problem to resolve; a risk is uncertainty. A change may be raised to address an issue or risk.
  13. Corrective, preventive, defect repair, update: know the four types.
  14. Do not let scope creep happen informally: route extras through the process.
  15. Emergency changes need a fast, authorized path and prompt documentation.
  16. Verify the results of an implemented change and record lessons.

12Exam Q&A

12.1 Scenario questions (choose the best answer)

S1During early planning of a hybrid project, before any baseline has been approved, stakeholders keep adjusting the draft scope, and a team member insists that every adjustment needs a formal change request. What is the correct view?

  • AFormal control starts with baselines; until then, refine the draft
  • BEvery adjustment needs a change request from the first day, to protect the project
  • CChanges are never formally controlled, even after the scope baseline has been approved
  • DOnly adjustments requested by the sponsor need to be recorded in the change log
Show the answer

Answer: A. A predictive project is not formally controlled until baselines exist; before that, drafts are refined and versions tracked, and once a baseline is approved all changes go through the formal process. Requiring requests from day one, never controlling or recording only sponsor requests misstates when and for whom control applies.

S2The change control board will decide on a design change in two weeks, and the team on the hybrid project asks whether to pause the affected work. What should the project manager do?

  • AAsk the team to wait and avoid any analysis until the decision arrives
  • BPause all related work until the board has made its decision
  • CKeep executing planned work while analyzing the impact of the change
  • DStart building the proposed change so that no time is lost if it is approved
Show the answer

Answer: C. While a decision is pending, the team continues the planned work and keeps analyzing the impact and risks of accepting or rejecting the change to limit negative effects. Pausing, starting early or idle waiting wastes time or implements an unapproved change.

S3An internal change board has approved a scope change, but the contract also requires the customer, who has no seat on that board, to approve scope changes. What should the project manager do?

  • AObtain the customer's approval before implementing the change
  • BTreat the customer's approval as optional if the sponsor agrees
  • CImplement the change now, because the board has already approved it
  • DAsk the customer to approve the change after it has been completed
Show the answer

Answer: A. Customer or sponsor approval may be needed after board approval unless they sit on the board, and a contractual requirement must be respected before implementation. Implementing first, treating approval as optional or seeking it afterward breaches the agreement.

S4A security vulnerability in the live product must be patched tonight, but the change control board meets next week. What is the best way to proceed?

  • AWait for next week's meeting, since the process must always be followed in order
  • BUse the emergency path with delegated authority, then document the change afterward
  • CApply the patch quietly and omit it from the change log to avoid questions
  • DAsk the vendor to apply the patch under the support contract with no record
Show the answer

Answer: B. Urgent changes for safety or security use an emergency path with delegated authority defined in advance, and the change is documented promptly afterward. Waiting for the board ignores the urgency, and skipping the record or the log removes accountability.

S5In an agile project, a stakeholder demands a formal approval letter before accepting that a request will not be built soon. What is the best approach?

  • ARemove the request from the backlog without telling the stakeholder
  • BIssue a formal rejection letter signed by the sponsor for every request
  • CShow the backlog ordering openly and explain where the request stands
  • DPromise to build the request in the next iteration to keep the stakeholder happy
Show the answer

Answer: C. In adaptive work a lower priority means the request is effectively deferred and not adding it means it is rejected, with no formal approval, so transparency about the backlog and its trade-offs keeps people informed. Letters, silent removal or false promises do not.

S6A change request lists only the extra cost of a feature. What else should be assessed before the decision?

  • AOnly the sponsor's opinion of the feature, since cost has already been estimated
  • BThe effect on the business case alone, because other areas follow from it
  • CNothing more, because cost is the only factor that the board needs to decide
  • DThe effect on schedule, scope, quality, risk, resources and stakeholders
Show the answer

Answer: D. Integrated change control assesses the impact on all domains, not only cost, with estimates of schedule and cost effects before any decision. Relying on cost alone, the sponsor's opinion or the business case alone leaves important effects unexamined.

S7Three months after a board-approved change went live, nobody has checked whether it delivered the intended effect. What should the project manager do?

  • ANothing, since an approved change is closed once it has been implemented
  • BReverse the change, since the lack of a check suggests that it failed
  • CMonitor the results, confirm the effect and record lessons
  • DAsk the board to approve the same change again so that it is recorded
Show the answer

Answer: C. The change process includes verifying that the change delivered its purpose, closing it in the log and recording lessons. Treating implementation as the end, reversing without evidence or seeking re-approval skips the verification.

S8A change adds one day and 500 to the budget, and the project manager's authority covers up to five days and 2,000. What should the project manager do?

  • ASend it to the change control board, since every change must go to the board
  • BAssess it and decide within authority, then log the decision
  • CAsk the sponsor to approve it, since sponsors approve all changes
  • DImplement it without recording it, because it is below the threshold
Show the answer

Answer: B. The project manager decides within the tolerance and authority set in the plan, and the board, sponsor or customer decide beyond it; every decision is logged. Escalating everything, skipping the log or involving the sponsor unnecessarily misuses the thresholds.

S9A team describes its change management plan as a program to help employees adopt a new system. According to PMBOK 8, what does a change management plan actually establish?

  • AThe rules for how stakeholders may be removed from the stakeholder register
  • BThe training and communication needed to move people to the future state
  • CThe schedule for deploying the new system to each department
  • DThe change control board, its authority and how the change control system works
Show the answer

Answer: D. In PMBOK 8 the change management plan sets up the change control board, its authority and the change control system, while helping people move to a future state is organizational change management. The other options describe training, deployment or stakeholder handling.

S10Which activity identifies configuration items, records their status and verifies the versions in use, as opposed to approving changes to them?

  • AScope validation, which obtains the customer's formal acceptance of the deliverables
  • BConfiguration management, which keeps the product configuration defined and verified
  • CChange control, which approves or rejects the changes requested to them
  • DQuality assurance, which audits whether processes comply with the standards
Show the answer

Answer: B. Configuration management identifies configuration items, records and reports their status and verifies versions, so the product stays consistent, whereas change control identifies, documents and approves or rejects changes. Assurance and validation are different activities.

S11Forty small approved changes to a hybrid project's baselined envelope have together added 18% to the budget, and the sponsor is surprised. What should the project manager have done?

  • AKept the changes out of status reports until the total reached 20%
  • BCombined the changes into a single request to avoid repeated approvals
  • CAsked the board to approve each change without any impact analysis
  • DReported pending and approved changes with their cumulative effect on the baselines
Show the answer

Answer: D. Status reports and dashboards show pending and approved changes and their cumulative effect on the baselines, so that small increments do not accumulate unnoticed. Combining requests, withholding information or approving without analysis hides the effect.

12.2 Recall Q&As

R1What are the four types of change request?

Show the answer

Corrective action, preventive action, defect repair and updates.

R2Who may request a change?

Show the answer

Any stakeholder, internally or externally.

R3What are the possible dispositions of a change request?

Show the answer

Approved, deferred or rejected (with a request for more information as a further outcome in the flow).

R4What does the change management plan define?

Show the answer

The change control board, its authority, and how the change control system is implemented.

R5What is a CCB?

Show the answer

A formally chartered group (also steering committee or project board) that reviews, evaluates, approves, defers or rejects changes and records and communicates decisions.

R6What is the difference between change control and configuration management?

Show the answer

Change control approves or rejects changes to documents, deliverables and baselines; configuration management identifies configuration items, records and reports their status and verifies and audits them.

R7When are changes formally controlled in predictive projects?

Show the answer

Once baselines are established, all changes go through the formal process.

R8How are changes managed in adaptive projects?

Show the answer

Through backlog management: a change becomes a backlog item with an impact analysis; priority decides; lower priority means deferred, not added means rejected.

R9What should a change request include before approval?

Show the answer

Estimated schedule and cost impacts (and other impacts) so the decision is informed.

R10What happens to deferred or rejected change requests?

Show the answer

They are recorded in the change log and communicated to the requester.

R11Which process implements approved changes?

Show the answer

Manage Project Execution.

R12What should the project manager do while waiting for a change decision?

Show the answer

Keep executing planned work and analyze the impact and risks of accepting or rejecting.

R13What may need updating after a change is approved?

Show the answer

Estimates, schedule, resources, risk assessments, baselines, plan components and project documents.

R14Why does "change management" need care on the exam?

Show the answer

PMBOK 8 uses "change management plan" for the CCB and change control system, while "change management" in the glossary means organizational transition; context decides.

13Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Process Assess and Implement Changes: from start to completion; any stakeholder may request
Types Corrective, preventive, defect repair, updates
Predictive Controlled once baselined; written request; impact on schedule and cost; CCB or approver: approved, deferred, rejected
Adaptive Backlog item; impact analysis; product owner prioritizes; lower = deferred, not added = rejected
Hybrid Formal control for the envelope; thresholds trigger approval
While waiting Keep executing planned work; analyze impact and risk
Communicate Change log; requester (including deferred and rejected); stakeholders; team
Implement Manage Project Execution; update baselines, plans, documents; verify
Documents Baselines, requirements, schedule, risks, backlog, contracts, versions; one controlled repository
No unapproved changes Even free improvements; submit retroactively
Baseline errors Fix through change control
Authority PM within tolerance; CCB, sponsor or customer beyond; define missing thresholds
Configuration management Identify items, status, verify, audit
Terminology Change management plan = CCB and control system; change management (glossary) = organizational transition
First-action pattern Document, assess impact, decide at the right level, communicate, implement, update documents, verify
